extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy fans (esp. performers considering international gigs)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, interviewer-framed guidance on what makes successful stand-up comedy and how to approach performing (material choices, platform, audience focus, and handling negative reactions). Geared toward comics working live and online, including international shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel‑good brand / effervescent stage persona
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘feel‑good brand of humour and effervescent smile’ — a consistent provider of laughs, chortles, and even the occasional hearty guffaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being known for a feel‑good vibe and warm stage presence helps ‘seduce the scene’ and reliably get audiences smiling; this is presented as a positive professional trademark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion for the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A man whose sheer passion for his craft is guaranteed to get you at the very least smiling along with him.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine passion is portrayed as essential to connect with audiences and sustain a comedy career; passion underpins consistent performance quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural humour versus class‑clownism
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To be a comedian you do have to have an element of natural humour to you, but being a class clown doesn’t always equate to being a great comedian.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural comedic sensibility is necessary but not sufficient; professional comedy requires more craft than simply being the class jokester (e.g., structure, timing, perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Banter and social intelligence as an edge
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I was the one that could always make the others laugh… being able to do that tends to give you an edge when it comes to certain situations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong conversational banter and the ability to make peers laugh are valuable skills that translate into stage advantages (audience connection, improvisation, social calibration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material universality with selective localization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A lot of the stuff I talk about are things which are pretty much universal… you should alter some of the more niche references but if you have to change your entire routine just to suit the crowd that means that your material isn’t as good as it should be.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write material around universal themes so it travels; adapt niche or region‑specific references as needed, but avoid wholesale rewrites of your core routine for each audience — overfitting material is a sign of weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right platform / 'know which lane to use'
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘As a comedian it’s important to know which lane to use now… the internet has meant that people no longer have to leave their homes to watch their favourite stand‑ups, it’s also added a bit of a new dynamic to the role of a comic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about whether material is developed for live shows or online clips; each platform has different demands (format, editing, punch timing) and requires strategic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise the live audience over chasing virality
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I would rather people come out to see me in person… If I were to do a comedy show on stage and my aim was “let me try and hit this joke for it to go viral” then I wouldn’t be properly focused on the crowd that was right in front of me.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform primarily for the paying, present audience; writing/performing to maximize online shares while live is an anti‑pattern that harms the immediate show experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and learn from negative audience reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: He was ‘booed off stage once’ on a program made for that — now he realises ‘that’s how the game of being a comedian works.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative responses (boos, walkouts) are part of the professional learning curve; treat them as expected setbacks and learning opportunities rather than career‑ending failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid low‑quality joke forms (e.g., knock‑knock jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I don’t think a genuinely funny knock‑knock joke even exists!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain joke formats are dismissed as inherently weak or juvenile; relying on such forms is implied to be poor practice for professional stand‑ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and using humour as a social tool
rubrics_metrics.description: He used humour to compensate for not being ‘very attractive as a child’ and is ‘a firm believer in keeping it real.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic self‑presentation and using humour honestly (rather than as a façade) are recommended; humour can serve as a genuine social lever but should remain sincere.
